content.content: RESEARCH ARTICLE [www.afm-journal.de](http://www.afm-journal.de) ![Image block](doc:468f0b8/tier:flash/page:1/block:3) # Energy-Efficient DUV Light Programming Nonvolatile Memory Based on MoS2/𝜷-Ga2O3/MLG Heterostructures for Neuromorphic Computing Jiang Zeng, Lin Hu, Yuan Pan, Zibin Huang, Huiru Sun, Jiexin Zeng, Xiuhua Xie,\* and Hongyu Chen\* **As one of the key components for brain-inspired computing, optoelectrical synapses based on memory devices are capturing growing attention due to their integrated function of sense and memory. However, the high power consumption (large programming voltage, high optical power density) and difficulty avoiding interference from solar radiation are potentially limiting their applications in artificial neural systems. Here, a novel optoelectrical floating gate memory based on molybdenum disulfide (MoS**2**)/𝜷-phase Gallium oxide (𝜷-Ga**2**O**3**)/Multilayer graphene is proposed. Benefitting from the unique photosensitive dielectric properties of 𝜷-Ga**2**O**3**, the device exhibits an excellent current switching ratio of 10**6 **only at a low programming/erasing voltage of ±40 V. Furthermore, the device possesses a strong anti-interference ability which can operate in the solar-blind region (254 nm) only with a low power of 254.4 pJ (0 V). Due to the large single photon energy at the short wavelength, the photon number (3.25 × 10**8**) used per programming operation is much smaller than that of most present works. The neural network model constructed with the memory device achieves an accuracy of 91.07% for image recognition. These results suggest the feasibility of constructing energy-efficient, anti-interference optoelectrical memory based on the van der Waals heterostructures for future artificial visual neuromorphic systems.** ## 1. Among them, the FG transistor is an ideal candidate for simulating synaptic functions with the ability of sensing, memory, and computation. Especially its three-terminal structure is highly advantageous for nondestructive weight updating and eliminates hidden current paths.[12] However, the majority of the present FG transistors mainly operate as electric-stimulated synaptic devices,[5,13–15] which are confronted with challenges of power consumption, thermal management, and anti-interference capability.[16–18] Optical signals offer a range of advantages over electrical signals, including low power consumption, low crosstalk, low computational requirements, and high bandwidth.[19,20] Consequently, optical-stimulated synaptic devices can be used to achieve a higher-performance data processing and communication system. Therefore, opticalstimulated artificial synapses based on FG transistors are urgently needed.[9,21–27] Although present commercial silicon-based optoelectrical FG transistors possess high comprehensive performance, these devices start to misbehave when their feature size shrinks toward several nanometers. It is because their active layer materials were generally constructed by several sophisticated instruments, such as molecular beam epitaxy (MBE), metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD), and atomic layer deposition (ALD), and sputtering, the inevitable defects will introduce and damage the semiconductor channel when the device is thinned. Fortunately, owing to their atomically thin thickness and dangling-bondfree characteristic, the emerging 2D materials show the great potential ability to sort out the way of these devices for “more than Moore”. As of yet, it is witnessed that the booming 2D FG optoelectrical memory devices with both long-term retention and multilevel storage capabilities exhibited unique Adv. Funct. Biological synapse in the human visual system and FG memory device. a) Schematic illustration of the human visual system, including information reception and information processing. b) Schematic diagram of the working process of the biological synapse (upper panel) and the proposed FG memory device (lower panel) based on MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/MLG van der Waals heterojunction. advantages such as fast speed and low power consumption in storage in constructing optic-stimulated artificial synapses.[12,28–30] As examples, 2D optoelectrical FG memory based on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) dielectric has aroused widespread interest in neuromorphic computing.[31–33] Bach et al. presented an optoelectronic memory based on rhenium disulfide (ReS2)/hBN/2D tellurene (Te) heterostructure, which was designed to enable reconfigurable inverter logic circuits through controlled electrical and optical inputs.[34] Gao et al. reported an optoelectronic memory based on 2D tin disulfide (SnS2)/hBN/Graphene heterostructure, which realized low optical writing energy and multibit storage.[35] Zha et al. introduced a multimodal reservoir computing system based on molybdenum disulfide (MoS2)/hBN/Te heterostructure for multimodal signal processing.[30] However, most of the aforementioned devices are still suffering high power consumption (large programming voltage, high optical power density), low on-off ratio and easily interfered with by solar radiation, which might restrict their use in artificial neural systems. To solve the above problems and explore novel energyefficient 2D FG memory with high performance, a novel energyefficient DUV light programming FG memory based on ultrathin MoS2/𝛽-phase Gallium oxide (𝛽-Ga2O3)/Multilayer graphene (MLG) is proposed based on our previous works.[36–38] To depict the schematics of the human visual system vividly, the working process including information reception and information processing is shown in **Figure 1**a. Unlike present FG memory used in neuromorphic systems, ultra-wide bandgap (4.9 eV) 𝛽-Ga2O3 with a high dielectric constant (ɛ = 10) and a high breakdown field (8 MV cm−1)[39–42] can function as a photosensitive dielectric in our device (Figure 1b), which not only could be functioned as an insulating dielectric layer in the dark blocking the carriers trapped in the FG but also excite photogenerated carriers under the deep-ultraviolet (DUV) radiation.[43–48] In addition, because the stratospheric ozone layer surrounding the earth absorbs high-energy ultraviolet radiation, our optoelectrical memory operating in the DUV solarblind region (220-280 nm) could avoid interference from solar radiation.[49–51] Therefore, the device shows excellent storage performance under electrical pulse, including a big current switching ratio of more than 106, large storage window ratio of 78.44%, excellent retention surpassing 103 s, and endurance exceeding 1000 programming/erasing cycles only with a low programming/erasing (P/E) voltage of ±40 V in a small equivalent electric field intensity of 7.94 MV cm−1.[52–56] Furthermore, the device was capable of achieving multilevel storage only by controlling the pulse DUV light (254 nm) with a low power of 254.4 pJ (0 V). And the number (3.25 × 108) of photons per programming operation is much smaller than that of most present works.[32–34,53,54,57,58] The distinctive mechanism indicates that our MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/MLG FG memory device holds great potential for optical memory, benefiting from strong anti-interference performance and reduction of dielectric layer losses due to the avoidance of tunneling mechanism. Finally, the MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/MLG FG memory device also demonstrates significant synaptic properties under photoelectric hybrid modulation, including synaptic short-term plasticity, pairpulse facilitation (PPF), and synaptic long-term plasticity. The VGG-8 model based on MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/MLG FG memory device achieves 91.07% recognition accuracy on CIFAR-10 dataset images. This work offers a new scheme for constructing an ultrathin neuromorphic storage and computing integrated system by using a DUV photosensitive dielectric. ## 2. To investigate the performance of the 2D 𝛽-Ga2O3 dielectric layer, a single MoS2 field effect transistor is realized by connecting MLG as a gate electrode, which is shown in Figure S2a (Supporting Information). And the transfer characteristics (Ids–Vcg) of the single MoS2 field effect transistor (FET) exhibit a typical n-type semiconductor behavior, with the threshold voltage (Vth) is −0.55 V when Vds = 1 V (Figure S2b, Supporting Information). Furthermore, the device demonstrates a high on/off ratio of 5 × 106 and electron mobility of 13.585 cm2 V−1 s−1 (Figure S3, Supporting Information). Our MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/MLG memory exhibits considerable potential in practical applications due to its exceptionally high stored charge density, which is generated by the increased barrier height between MLG and 𝛽-Ga2O3. The switching ratios at different pulse widths when the P/E voltage is ±40 V and Vds = 1 V are exhibited in Figure 3f. An evident trend of increasing difficulty in P/E operations is observed with decreasing pulse widths, Figure S5 (Supporting Information) suggests that an ideal P/E operating pulse width of 0.1 s for the device is optimal, as it allows for a high on/off ratio of 5 × 106 to be tightly controlled. In addition, Figure 3g illustrates the switching ratios at different P/E voltages with the pulse width of 0.1 s and Vds = 1 V. Obviously, when the pulse voltage decreases, the convenience of the P/E operations will diminish. Further details, as depicted in Figure S6 (Supporting Information), reveal that the optimal P/E operating voltage for the device is ±40 V, as this voltage ensures the maintenance of a high on/off ratio of 5 × 106, thereby underscoring the device’s operational efficiency and reliability. And the retention stability of the programming and erasing states was measured at Vbg = 0 V and Vds = 1 V, respectively, after applying ±40 V/0.1 s electrical pulse (Figure 3h). Throughout an extended retention period exceeding 103 s, the currents of state-0 and state-1 demonstrated tremendous stability. And the anticipated retention currents of the device for over 10 years are shown in Figure S7 (Supporting Information). The expected retention time of the current ratio between the two states exceeds 103, indicating that the FG memory device has excellent retention capability. The endurance characteristics of the memory device determined by repeated programming and erasure cycles are shown in Figure 3i, the device successfully completed more than 1000 programming/erasing cycles with a negligible decay in the Ids, confirming high endurance and long-term stability of our FG memory device. The schematic energy-band diagrams of four processes are illustrated in Figure 3j. Initially, when a +40 V gate voltage is applied, electrons will tunnel through 𝛽-Ga2O3 and transfer to the graphene FG. Subsequently, when the gate voltage is eliminated to read the state-0 current, the substantial electron accumulation in the graphene FG is interpreted by the MoS2 channel as a negative gate voltage, consequently driving the MoS2 channel into off-state. What’s more, when a −40 V gate voltage is used to erase, the electrons in graphene will be transferred to the MoS2 channel, thereby forcing the MoS2 channel into an on-state. Thus, the MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/MLG FG memory is capable of realizing two-level non-volatile storage by electrostatic control. Apart from its competitive performance of electrical memory devices, 𝛽-Ga2O3 can also function as a photosensitive high-𝜅 dielectric layer, due to the combination of high dielectric constant and excellent optoelectronic properties. The photoresponse characteristics of a MoS2 FET and a MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/MLG FG memory device were investigated under the dual influence of electrical pulsing and photonic irradiation, with 𝛽-Ga2O3 serving as the photosensitive high-𝜅 dielectric layer. The schematic illustration of MoS2 FET with 𝛽-Ga2O3 is shown in Figure S8a (Supporting Information). And time-resolved Igs curves of the MoS2 FET at Vb =−5 V under 405 nm are shown in Figure S8c (Supporting Information). Notably, the Igs remains at a minimal level of ∼10−14 A under visible light, which underscores the significant applicability of 𝛽-Ga2O3 for high-𝜅 dielectric applications. Additionally, as depicted in Figure S8d, the obvious photoresponse of Igs to 254 nm light on/off switching cycles underscores the inherent UV-sensitive characteristic of the 𝛽- Ga2O3 at Vcg =−5 V under 254 nm, indicating its significant potential as an efficient photosensitive dielectric. Furthermore, the schematic energy-band diagrams of the optoelectronic behavior are illustrated in Figure S8b. In dark conditions, the 𝛽-Ga2O3 functions as a high-𝜅 dielectric layer with minimal leakage current, allowing for precise regulation of the channel’s carrier density and surface potential through the application of Vcg.[69] The MoS2 channel uniquely generates a substantial quantity of photogenerated carriers under 405 nm, however, the Igs remain unaffected as these carriers are incapable of tunneling through the 𝛽-Ga2O3 dielectric layer. Conversely, upon exposure to 254 nm light, the wide-bandgap 𝛽-Ga2O3 exhibits a significant response to UV light under 254 nm illumination, which results in a significant enhancement of photogenerated carriers. At the control of Vcg =−5 V, the photogenerated electrons within the 𝛽- Ga2O3 layer are transferred to the conduction band of MoS2, leading to a marked response in Igs. Consequently, the unique photosensitive characteristics of the high-𝜅 dielectric 𝛽-Ga2O3 introduce a novel optoelectronic mechanism within FG memory devices. In the realm of non-volatile memory devices, the tunneling effect predominates as the mechanism for device programming. However, the endurance of such devices is often compromised following repeated cycles of erasure and programming. Storage mechanisms that eschew tunneling may provide a viable solution to this durability conundrum.[70,71] Consequently, the MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/MLG FG memory device could achieve optical programming by applying DUV light. The application of an initial erasing pulse at −30 V for 0.01 s facilitates the transfer of electrons from graphene to the MoS2 channel, preventing their subsequent tunneling back and thereby generating an internal electric field between the MoS2 channel and the graphene floating gate layer. As illustrated in Figure S9 (Supporting Information), the photogenerated electrons cannot transit into the floating gate due to the absence of an internal electric field, hence the programming operation cannot be realized solely by applying 254 nm light pulses. Additionally, Figure 4e and Figure S10 (Supporting Information) demonstrate the programming operation using 1 s pulses of 405, 635, and 520 nm respectively. And it reveals that the photosensitive dielectric layer of 𝛽-Ga2O3 fundamentally limits electron tunneling under visible light illumination, which will not be affected by the disturbance of visible light. The schematic energy-band diagrams of electrical erasing and 405 nm light programming are illustrated in Figure 4c. When the visible light pulse is applied, only the MoS2 channel excites electrons from the valence band, and these photogenerated electrons cannot tunnel through 𝛽-Ga2O3, leading to a noticeable increase in output current instead of a decrease during programming. In Figure 4f, the device is successfully programmed by 254 nm/1 s light pulse, with reading states measured at Vbg = 0V and Vds = 1 V. The capability for multilevel storage within the FG memory is demonstrated by augmenting the quantity of light pulses. The schematic energy-band diagrams of electrical erasing and DUV light programming are visualized in Figure 4d. Upon application of an electrical pulse with a voltage of −30 V for 0.01 s, electrons initially tunnel through 𝛽-Ga2O3 and migrate to the MoS2 channel, completing the erasing operation. Subsequently, following the removal of the gate voltage, a significant accumulation of holes occurs in the graphene, which the MoS2 channel interprets as a positive gate voltage, thereby maintaining an on-state. Subsequently, DUV light (254 nm) with pulse widths of 1 s is used for programming, which could excite electrons from the valence bands of both 𝛽-Ga2O3 and MoS2, leading to the generation of electron-hole pairs. However, it is noted that only the carriers originating from 𝛽-Ga2O3 are capable of transiting into either channel or FG. Within the graphene FG, the electrons will be neutralized with holes, effectively reducing the gate voltage, whereas in the MoS2 channel, the holes will recombine with the electrons, reducing the lifetime of the majority carriers. Consequently, the FG memory achieves programming operation through the 254 nm light pulse, whereas carriers originating from MoS2 encounter significant challenges in penetrating the dielectric layer. The comparative influence of optical depression pulses with pulse widths of 2 and 0.5 s on the output current is illustrated in Figure S11 (Supporting Information). The degree of programming is indicated to increase with the duration of light exposure. In Figure S12 (Supporting Information), additional samples with the different thickness of 𝛽-Ga2O3 layer exhibited excellently programmed ability under the pulse light of 254 nm, thereby providing further corroboration of the photosensitive mechanism to the 𝛽-Ga2O3 dielectric layer.[41,72] And it can be known that a thicker dielectric layer demands a higher pulse voltage to attain the same current level, leading to increased power consumption. Furthermore, it can be found that in Table S1 (Supporting Information), the MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/MLG FG memory is capable of achieving multilevel storage only by controlling the pulse DUV light (254 nm) with a low power of 254.4 pJ. Owing to the elevated potential barrier between the FG layer and the dielectric layer, coupled with the exceptional insulating characteristics of 𝛽-Ga2O3. As shown in Figure 4g,h, the device exhibits an excellent current switching ratio of 106 only at a low programming/erasing voltage of ±40 V in a small equivalent electric field intensity of 7.94 MV cm−1,[34,73,74] meanwhile displaying a tiny photons number of 3.25 × 108, which is much smaller than that of most present works as well.[32,33,53,54] Synaptic plasticity, which refers to the ability of synapses to change the efficiency of transmitting signals in biological synapses, is mainly manifested as the correlation between the changes in postsynaptic membrane polarization degree and electrical signal retention time and the stimulus signals. According to the length of retention time, it can be divided into shortterm plasticity (STP) and long-term plasticity (LTP). As shown in **Figure 5**a and Figure S13 (Supporting Information), with the increase of pulse amplitude and number, the magnitude and retention time of the postsynaptic current (PSC) also increases, which is consistent with the phenomenon that the human brain forms a more profound and firm memory after reinforcement and repeated stimulation.[75] The one potentiation ratio is defined as the ratio of the PSC before the electrical pulse and the PSC after the pulse (Ibefore/Iafter). One potentiation ratio with different pulse widths was tested, as Figure 5b shows. As a typical type of STP, paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) refers to the phenomenon that the excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) of the post-synapse after the second stimulation is significantly larger than the EPSC after the first stimulation when a pair of identical consecutive pulses are applied to stimulate the synapse. By applying two identical consecutive electrical pulses, the EPSC at different pulse intervals (Δt) is shown in Figure S14 (Supporting Information). The EPSC of the device after the second electrical pulse (A2) is significantly larger than that after the first electrical pulse (A1), indicating that the continuous stimulation has a facilitative effect on synaptic weights. The degree of facilitation can be quantitatively assessed using the formula PPF = A2/A1. The trend of PPF changing with Δt is shown in Figure 5c. It can be seen that with the increase of Δt, the PPF index shows a regular decline, which is similar to the behavior of biological synapses. Conclusion Herein, a novel energy-efficient DUV light programming FG memory based on ultrathin MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/Multilayer graphene (MLG) was fabricated. Due to the unique optoelectronic characteristics and high dielectric constant of 𝛽-Ga2O3, our FG memories with robust anti-interference capabilities could achieve multilevel storage under DUV light only with a low power of 254.4 pJ (254 nm, 0 V). And due to the large single photon energy at the short wavelength, the photon number (3.25 × 108) used per programming operation is much smaller than that of most present works. In addition, the device also demonstrates remarkable storage performance including a substantial current switching ratio exceeding 106, a significant storage window ratio of 78.44%, exceptional retention surpassing 103 s, and endurance exceeding 1000 programming/erasing cycles under a low programming/erasing (P/E) voltage of ±40 V. Ultimately, by mapping the LTP/LTD currents under photoelectric hybrid modulation into synaptic weights, a VGG-8 neural network model was constructed utilizing MoS2/𝛽- Ga2O3/MLG FG memory devices, which could achieve an accuracy of 91.07% for the image recognition in the CIFAR-10 dataset. In summary, the innovative design provided new insights for the van der Waals heterostructure optical memory devices based on the Ga2O3 photosensitive dielectric, which in turn provides a new building block for constructing energyefficient artificial visual neuromorphic systems with high performance. ## 4. Experimental Section Device Fabrication: The MLG, MoS2 nanosheets were obtained by mechanical exfoliation (3 M Scotch tape) from the bulk (from Shanghai On-Way Technology Co., Ltd.). The MoS2/𝛽-Ga2O3/MLG FG memory was fabricated on SiO2/Si substrate with a dry transfer method with the transparent polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) film. First, MLG, 𝛽-Ga2O3, and MoS2 were exfoliated from their crystals with Scotch tape. Then, the devices were spin-coated with positive photoresist (ARP-5350 was purchased from Taizhou SUNANO New Energy Co., Ltd.) and obtained electrode patterns by UV exposure via an Ultraviolet Maskless Lithography machine (TuoTuo Technology (Suzhou) Co., Ltd.). Finally, 10 nm Cr and 50 nm Au layers were deposited onto the devices employing the electron beam evaporation instrument as contact electrodes. Device Characterization: Raman spectroscopy (invia) with a laser wavelength of 532 nm was used to confirm the materials. The optical microscope diagrams were obtained by optical microscopy (BA3 10MET-T, Motic) and AFM (Dimension FastScan from Bruker Co.,Ltd). The electrical and optoelectronic characteristics of the devices were performed at room temperature via a four-probe station with two source meters (Keithley 2636B system and Keithley 2611B system). The optoelectronic measurements were performed by various laser sources (405, 520, and 635 nm). And the 254 nm light was produced by the LED lamp. ## Supporting Information Supporting Information is available from the Wiley Online Library or from the author. ## Acknowledgements J.Z. and L.H. contributed equally to this work.
